There seem to be prescriptions for having the make-up air close, and others for being a ways away. Architect wants to incorporate that into the hood or as a curtain, but based on some reading, that may not be a sound approach. other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "kaseki", "author_name": "kaseki", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/kaseki", "date": "2022-11-01", "text": "The goal is to introduce the MUA in a manner that does not cause turbulence at the hood thereby causing the rising and expanding cooking plumes to spread beyond the hood canopy capture area.  (See Hart and Cooley web site for 'register' vs. 'diffuser.')  https://www.hartandcooley.com/ If introduced near or at the hood, it should be through a diffuser aiming the flow away from the hood across the ceiling where it can mix with the room air as it flows through it and as it turns at the opposite wall. If introduced well away from the hood in the kitchen, a register dumping it downward may do. If in an adjacent long hallway, then a diffuser aimed at the hood may help keep the flow more laminar than turbulent If via a large space worth of toe-kick panels, then registers should be OK so long as the toe-kick flows do not interact with adjacent cabinets causing local (to the hood) turbulence. You should aim for 90 CFM/sq. ft. of hood entry area; and this makes the blower zero static pressure flow rate requirement about 1.5X this.  Tepid cooking on induction may allow a lower maximum flow rate.", "images": []}}

The tented design, as in my Wolf Pro Island hood shown below, is very modest in volume, so my opinion is that the flow rate should be based on baffle gap air entrainment velocity requirements and not depend on much averaging.  Commercial hoods with deliberately large reservoirs below the baffles can make full use of the volume for averaging the plume(s) over the entire baffle space (typically only one sided). Tilted baffles tend to move grease to the lower ends, but how important this is depends on how much greasy stuff one cooks. Subtleties of air flow can allow or not having physical hood boundaries larger than the baffle space but yet include it all in the effective capture area.  For the 1-inch-ish edges of my hood, the air flow is sufficient to count that area, in my opinion.  The light bar is probably only partially fully efficient, so I don't usually count it.  Baffle frames, holders, etc. that are inside the boundary will not reflect plume portions out of the hood if the flow rate is sufficient. These plants are grown overseas (in the tropics, to save heating and cooling costs), and for the most part are grown using automated culture. When the plant is blooming and ready for sale, the plastic pots are removed from the growing racks and placed in decorative ceramic pots much like the one you show with the plant in the photo. These decorative cover pots are to protect the plants while in shipment, and make them look more attractive to sell better.  The decorative cover pots usually do not have drainage holes in them, and in my opinion are one of the main reason many people have so much difficulty growing orchids. The clerks in the \u201cbig box\u201d stores are told to water the plants when they get dry, but no one knows how important it is to pour the standing water out of the outer pots after watering. Roots in standing water = root rot. Orchids grow very slowly, so it can sometimes take as much as a month for root rot to become apparent in a plant, and the first signs are a limp dehydrated plant which is exactly what root rot is. No roots, no water intake, so the inexperienced grower starts watering the plant more, when in fact the best remedy is to take the plant out of the pot and dry it out and try to save any remaining roots, and grow new ones. Does the pot you show beside the plant have drainage holes (hole) in the bottom? If not, don\u2019t even consider putting your plant in it. Try to find a clay (orchid) pot. Orchid pots have slits cut in the side of the pot in addition to the hole in the bottom. These allow excellent drainage and air to circulate around the roots. If you can\u2019t find clay, then a plastic \u201cazalea\u201d pot is next best. The azalea pots are not as deep as a \u201cstandard\u201d pot, so are easier to dry out between watering. I personally would remove the bloom spike from the plant. It might branch and produce a few more blooms, but in my opinion the previous owner got their money\u2019s worth out of that one, and its time for you to encourage the plant to produce a new spike for you. Use a sterile sharp razor knife, and cut the stem leaving a stump about an inch long. You can put fungicide on the cut if you want to- lots do, lots don\u2019t. South facing window is ok, no direct (hot) sunlight, and 55-60 degrees F. minimum night temp. Use orchid bark mix with fir bark as the primary ingredient. Wet the bark before potting. Take the plant out of the pot and remove any dead roots. (dried papery looking, usually covering a hard dried stick like central stem.)  If you cut into live tissue, same procedure as for cutting the bloom spike. Fungicide is more important here since most folks won\u2019t let the roots get really dry before potting. I usually unpot the plant today, and trim it up and repot tomorrow to let the plant get really dry before I start working on it. Cover the roots well with the wet bark mix and make sure to fill in all air pockets. When potted, put the plant in a warm shady spot and let it dry out thoroughly \u2013 several days before beginning its regular watering schedule. Let it get almost completely dry before watering it normally. You do not have to use \u201corchid fertilizer\u201d, the numbers are what count. 30-10-10 high nitrogen (first number) makes the plant grow. Before I expect blooming, I shift to a balanced fertilizer, 10-10-10, etc. all numbers the same. There are almost as many theories on fertilizer usage as there are orchid growers, so use what works. Hope this helps. Just remember, orchids are \u201ctough old birds\u201d, I suggest getting a culture book and use that as a guideline. The American Orchid Society is a good source. Come back here if you want to talk through a problem, just remember, here you get all levels of experience, and folks living all over the world telling you how they do it. Body Bags This \u201cbag\u201d stands on the ground and has a shape of an actual person, fully with arms, body, and face. title: Approaching Owner of Home Not for Sale | Houzz Forum

That said, we're ultimately happy we didn't go through with building, but unfortunately the housing market is a little wonky right now which makes buying difficult. We've found a house that we really like in the town we live in, the catch is that it's not for sale and actually recently sold this past June of 2022. This may sound like a no-go right away, but after some research, we've found out that the people who bought the house live on the other side of the country and are using it as an air bnb rental during the summer and a college rental during the winter, so there's no real emotional attachment that we can tell. From what we've gleaned, it seems like they're trying to start some sort of air bnb empire to more or less success. The bottom line is that the house seems like primarily or entirely an investment property. The house (and ourselves) are located in a little rural town with a college and a small lake. Over the years the area has fluctuated in popularity. In the 30's-50's it was a pretty popular vacation town, after that it became rather dismal with a lot of rundown houses. Recent years has seen an upswing in popularity, but summer rentals seem like they're slowing down in popularity again and our college enrollment is way down which isn't good for student rentals. Over the entire summer we saw only a handful of vacationers (or anyone) there and we've noted that the property isn't maintained frequently with weeds growing up the side of the house and the lawn getting shin high or higher before someone takes care of it. We really like the house for a variety of reasons, a major one being that it's within walking distance of family, and are trying to figure out how to approach the situation. The offer we're thinking of making is 50k-70k more than what they bought it for in June. We're hopeful that because it seems to be an investment property they'll be more interested in taking the money and reinvesting it in another house instead of holding out for long-term rental gains in an uncertain rental market. All that said, I'm looking for advice on how to go about composing a letter to these people. We have their address and names, but we need to come up with something that comes across as serious without being rude or mushy, etc. Basically we're trying to figure out how to draft an attractive letter of interest, though if you have any other advice/suggestions/insight I wouldn't mind hearing that either. title: Dangerous? Just unpacked old R-209F Sharp 800-watt microwave-oven | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "jally1", "author_name": "jally", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/jally1", "date": "2022-11-04", "text": "I've had a 1980s 700watt Sharp microwave that was so wonderful, it lasted this long, but then the spring-mechanism for the push-button door-opener had steadily weakened, so now I can't use it, even though everything else is still fine. So because of that, I unpacked a \"newer\" yet still-vintage, spare (Walmart-bought) R-209F Sharp 800-watt microwave oven. Because its an old model, perhaps 20 years old, its way way past warranty. There's no comparison between the latter, turn-of-century Sharp, and the 1980s one. The 1980s one was genuine, the former is JUNK, as the keypad-panel has very inferior operational function, or none at all, to the point of downright danger! To clarify: I'd tried defrosting a pita bread. so I pressed the key which stated FROZEN-ENTREES, figuring that after a short time, I'd merely click STOP and check how defrosted it is. But the STOP key failed to work! It only seems to work when, for example, you've set the timer and wish to stop that, or else if you set the clock and wish to stop that. So I was frantic, since there was a long way left to go, and I'd begun seeing smoke billowing inside the microwave - probably from the powder of the pita. So because i was desperate, I manually pulled the door-handle open, and only then did it stop. But by then, a permanent brownish burn-smudge had appeared below the keypad-panel. And this week, yet again, I found myself having to manually pull it open, for yet another miscalculation. So my question is, whether it's dangerous to manually pull open the door while it's running? My concern is regarding radiation.", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "kaseki", "author_name": "kaseki", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/kaseki", "date": "2022-11-05", "text": "The oldest (and only) Sharp microwave oven that I have rooted around in was a 2007 OTC model.  It has multiple door interlock switches.  I was happy to prove that even with one switch bad (fan and light stayed on with the door open), the microwave power was off. I have the microwave power meter that Sharp recommends for testing their units for leakage.  It read no power (within its sensitivity range) outside the unit, even with the unit's skin removed.  I had to put the probe inside the electronics bay (not the oven cavity) next to the light bulb to get some meter action.  So I think you are safe in that brief moment when the door is cracked and the field is collapsing, because the gap is still too small.  However, it is possible for multiple switch failures to cause an exposure, so if pulling the door open doesn't stop operation of light, turntable, and/or fan, then further inspection is warranted. Buying a new oven may be justified, as the cost of even a used test meter is commensurate with typical microwave oven costs.  And I assure everyone that the time value required to tear apart the oven to replace a microswitch (plus that of obtaining the microswitch) is likely to exceed the replacement cost of the oven.  On the other hand, one does get access to clean the guts after years of operation. This question reminds me that WiFi operates in this band, and I should dig out that meter and see what it reads with a \"tp-link\" that I use when I need to update my cell 'phone software.  Otherwise, I don't have WiFi running, so I hope my message above doesn't mislead the reader into believing that I am cavalier about bathing in microwave radiation.", "images": []}}

They are harmless to the plant but may be an indication that watering is on the heavy side.", "images": []}, "Comment 2": {"author_id": "ken-adrian", "author_name": "ken_adrian Adrian MI cold Z5", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/ken-adrian", "date": "2022-11-05", "text": "you are on the verge of loving your plant to death.. since you brought it home.. youve reduced the canopy.. repotted it.. put it in the basement.. severely reducing light levels.. and you change watering protocol .. how about you just water it properly .. and otherwise leave it alone for 2 or 3 months .. and then decide if its over all the stress inflicted on it ... house is warm enough.. dont care about the window cold.. unless the window ices up..and the leaves are actually touching the ice/window ... the heat register could dry media surface while leave the lower media wet.. so learn how to FEEL the weight of water in the pot.. and water when it drys thru the whole pot... what gal said on the mold/fungus being media related. not plant related.. ignore is.. or just scratch it off with a spoon ... ken", "images": []}, "Comment 3": {"author_id": "webuser-355114", "author_name": "tapla  (mid-Michigan, USDA z5b-6a)", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/webuser-355114", "date": "2022-11-05", "text": "Several things can cause holes/tears in the leaves. The most obvious would be mechanical injury (for animals - like a bruise). Sometimes though, dry air/ low relative humidity can cause leaf surfaces to stick to each other while the leaf is still furled and yet to fully emerge, so \"right under the heat vent\" is a concern. The counterpart to photo synthesis, the process by which plants make their own food (sugar/ glucose), is respiration, during which the food/ energy created is used. Increasing temperatures and decreasing humidity can significantly increase the rate of respiration, so much, in fact, that it causes the plant to use more food/ energy than the plant can create. This is an unsustainable arrangement that can have serious consequences for the plant. The other potentiality would be the plant's inability to maintain a steady supply of calcium in the nutrient stream. Only some nutrients are mobile in the plant, that is to say the plant can only mobilize and move certain nutrients from place to place within the plant. Nitrogen, phosphorous, potassium, and magnesium are mobile in the plant. The remainder are only somewhat immobile or immobile in the plant, meaning the immobile nutrients must be in the nutrient stream at all times if cells (and particularly cell walls) are to form normally. Soggy soils limit calcium uptake, causing weak cell walls and abnormal cells. When many cells are affected, it forms weak spots in tissues that cause holes and tears. This can occur as the result of a true deficiency due to an actual inadequate supply of calcium in the soil, or it can be a cultural deficiency, during which a cultural condition inhibits uptake of calcium from what could be an adequate supply; thus, a culturally caused calcium deficiency. If you actually saw fungus gnats flying around the plant, that would tend to add support to the idea the grow medium holds too much water, or, you're watering too frequently. BTW - it is best practice if you do not allow any water to remain in the collection saucer after a thorough watering. If no water collects in the saucer, you're not watering thoroughly. If water does collect and remain in the saucer, you are ensuring that all salts from tapwater and fertilizer solutions remain in the soil where they eventually cause the plant's inability to take up enough water to keep the plant properly hydrated. The white filaments on the soil are fungal hyphae. If you notice, they occur where there is the least amount of air movement due to the movement being slowed considerably by the stems. This also contributes weight to the idea you might be over-watering. The fungal hyphae are not in themselves a concern, as plants live in harmony with thousands of fungal species. Like Gardengal mentioned, the concern has more to do with the over-watering that might be occurring chronically. Almost all commonly grown herbaceous houseplants in the Northern Hemisphere are best repotted in the 2-3 weeks immediately before the summer solstice (21 June). This is because they will (or should) have a high level of reserve food/ energy, and, their current ability to create food/ energy will be peaking. This means recovery at that time will be quicker than at any other point during the growth period. Repotting in fall, winter, early spring should be avoided because low light and short days increases recovery time considerably, leaving plants more vulnerable to insect herbivory and biotic/ abiotic pathogens. Plants are most vulnerable in terms of energy depletion in mid-winter through early spring. Al", "images": []}}

The goal with hanging drywall is to have as few seams as possible when hanging.  You have a very very badly finished seams and they tried to cover it up with badly applied stippling .  The seams should have  been taped, mudded,  feathered out and sanded. You are never going to match the present stippling.  Definitely done by someone who never done drywall before.  The waving is probably due to not enough drywall screws per each sheet. My guess would be they used drywall nails instead of drywall screws because they are cheaper. I've been listening to his best-selling book \"The Power of Now\" on Audible and find myself actually exclaiming aloud, \"so true!\" to many of his points.  Mindfulness, being in the now, achieving a more enlightened state of being at my core ... these are things that have greatly sparked my interest as of late, and I'd like to chat about it with anyone who is like-minded.  I'm sure that some here have considerable knowledge in this arena and can recommend excellent teachers and practices. As I continue on my religious deconstruction journey, I am intrigued by aspects of eastern spiritualism and mysticism.  Having grown up in a religion that I thought was vastly different than these things (and in certain aspects is), I do find many corollaries between the ideologies of those considered the greatest teachers to ever walk the planet. What has happened and what will happen ... these do not exist.  All that is real is the here, the now, this very moment, and I'm beginning to see the great importance of centering back to the here/now instead of letting my mind meander all over the place.  For so much of my life, I have considered it something of an \"art\" to have such a well-developed \"inner life\".  Even as a child, I could entertain myself for hours on end remembering things or focusing on what might come and dwelling on the future.  I had a very active imagination.  I now understand why this is deemed illusory, and I long for something more.  It isn't even easy to put all of this into words -- not adequately, certainly.  But those who have had any positive exposure to this thinking whatsoever will surely understand what I'm trying to convey. The more I recenter myself into this present moment, the more everything else simply melts away.  This has already been helpful to me in everyday situations - like being stuck in traffic. main_question: {"author_id": "editoria", "author_name": "Alisande", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/editoria", "date": "2022-11-08", "text": "I made these in 2019 for my grandsons to give to their parents on Christmas, and I'm going to do it again this year. What was the best part of  your summer vacation? What's your favorite food? What's your hardest subject in school? and so on . . . Type up their answers (\"My favorite teacher is Mrs. Crankshaft\") and leave space around them so you can cut them out. You'll end up with a bunch of paper strips that you'll put into clear plastic ball ornaments. But first, take a picture--a headshot--of each child, and print it in a size that will fit nicely in the ornament. If you can photograph them holding a sign stating the year 2022, all the better. If not, or if you are cutting out an existing photo, use a marker to write the year on card stock. That will go in the ornament too. So you'll end up with a clear plastic ball containing a picture of the child, the current year, and lots of strips of paper that tell about this child in this year. Specific hoods are not listed, so this should be treated as somewhat qualitative. 801642 1200 CFM  0.2 in at 420 CFM; 0.4 at 600 CFM; 0.7 at 800 CFM (840 CFM max) 801641  900 CFM  0.2 at 420 CFM; 0.4 at 600 CFM; 0.7 at 800 CFM  (760 CFM max) 801640  600 CFM 0.2 at 420 CFM; 0.4 at 600 CFM (540 CFM is max with this blower) Essentially, the fan curves change, but the pressure loss with flow rate does not change, so these are plotted for the same hood.  And I don't know if it is the one I have (66 in. Pro Island). I extended these (this) pressure loss curve on a 1500 CFM blower fan curve and got 1 inch, w.c., at 1000 CFM. Note that I have a 1500 CFM blower and I have measured roughly 1000 CFM at the hood with 10-inch duct, silencer, three maybe 60-deg bends, and perhaps 20 ft. of duct. Hoods of the same design (e.g., Wolf Pro Island) will, for the same CFM per baffle assembly, have the same pressure loss. I recall Fantech informing me of the pressure loss, but I would have to dig deep to find the information.  The silencers have an internal diameter equal to the duct size, so only turbulence around the internal perforations to the sound chamber would have any effect beyond smooth duct. title: butcher block countertop advice | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "webuser-913321892", "author_name": "HU-913321892", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/webuser-913321892", "date": "2022-11-09", "text": "Hi all: I would like to install solid wood (birch? oak?) butcher block countertops in my kitchen. The cheaper the better ;) (Does ikea sell?) Any recommendations?  also- should i seal with waterlox? or leave unfinished and just oil? Additionally, if anyone has experience with butcher block countertops (especially with young children) feel free to chime in! this kitchen will probably last 7-10 years tops as we plan to either gut it or move at some point. thanks!", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "pfvwus-pf~1481101927", "author_name": "User", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/professionals/pfvwus-pf~1481101927", "date": "2022-11-09", "text": "Butcher block is something that the good is very good, and lasts for generations.  And the bad is very bad, and lasts for maybe a few years.  Good butcher block is end grain maple, like John Boos sells. It's going to be the price equivalent to a higher granite or quartz.  The low end \"wood counters\" like Lumber Liquidators or Lowes sell are face grain, rubberwood or the like, with a lot of glue.  Sniff what you're interested in buying. It should smell like wood, not chemicals. Some of the low end smells pretty terrible. Either way, the waterproofing around a cut for a sink will need to be a regular upkeep issue.  The back side of the counter needs treating, as well as the cut edge and top.  Every couple of years needs the sinks dropped, and the underneath scraped and sanded and treated, with new silicone between the sink and wood. Otherwise, there are too many plants to name that would enjoy a sunny windowsill over winter.", "images": []}, "Comment 5": {"author_id": "webuser-355114", "author_name": "tapla  (mid-Michigan, USDA z5b-6a)", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/webuser-355114", "date": "2022-11-09", "text": "You should find this to be helpful: Much Ado about Container Media If you have access to bark of appropriate size, mixing in some peat, perlite, and dolomitic (garden) lime will provide you with a very productive medium. main_question: {"author_id": "skindigo", "author_name": "Michelle", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/skindigo", "date": "2022-11-11", "text": "I am seriously considering the Wolf Induction 36\" cooktop CIT36YB for my kitchen reno.  My biggest concern at this juncture is the size of the actual coil, magnet, hob (or whatever it is called LOL)  Not necessarily the size of the circle etched on the glass, but the hob under the glass.  My understanding is that the size of the coil is what determines what size skillets will work best.  A coil less than 9\" will not heat a 12\" skillet from edge to edge properly.  If you have this unit please let me know what your experience has been.  Thanks so much!", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "mcarroll16", "author_name": "mcarroll16", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/mcarroll16", "date": "2022-11-12", "text": "1. Base size on the 15\" pan is 12 1/2\". 2. Not even edge-to-edge heat. I don't cook much meat, so I can't give detailed notes on the variation. I'm mostly sauteeing large batches of veggies in that pan. But I do sometimes use a modified stir-fry technique where I move some things to the edge for slower cooking, other things to the middle for more intense heat. One factor though is that the skillet is a bit curved across the bottom. My slightly smaller stainless skillets have a bottom diameter that matches the burner size, and are flatter. They are very even. 3. Noises--sometimes. It's mostly the All Clad, which matches up what others have said about multi-ply pans. And it's usually kind of mis-match issue--putting a large stockpot on a small burner on very high heat. In those cases there is sometimes a whistle or a rattle or both. We had laminate counters previously, now we have quartz. Maybe that amplifies the sound? But it's pretty rare that I notice it. 4. I would absolutely always choose induction over gas. It's faster and more responsive. It's much safer for my kids (I have a special-needs kid who loves to cook). And it's much healthier. I have asthma, so my doctors recommend no gas cooktop ever. title: Anyone Else Want to Share a "Covid Wedding" story? | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "barncatz", "author_name": "barncatz", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/barncatz", "date": "2022-11-12", "text": "Too soon?  I hope not. Jinx's wedding thread reminded me of DD's 8/2020 Covid wedding. It was supposed to happen in a small hotel (shut down) shortly after her MFA ceremony (canceled). We hopefully rescheduled with the hotel for four months later (HA!). The florist, wedding cake were from outside vendors so they got cancelled. Guests got invites, cancellations, second invites, third invites/cancellations of second invites. DD had carefully researched Covid literature and noted that outdoor infections were vanishly small, so we rented a gorgeous farm venue in late August 2020 and crossed our fingers. Everyone was still worried about contact infections, so wine, beer and soft drinks were individual bottles kept on ice and picked up as desired.  We found a caterer willing to do a State Fair type food booth for people to pick up their own food in the individual baskets we provided anytime during the event. We had a \"make a rootbeer float\" table with individual ice cream servings in a freezer so that people didn't have to share containers or scoops, and individual cans of rootbeer. We marked off the line area with six foot distance markers. We had a cake for decoration but served cupcakes so people could approach the table individually for their individually handled dessert. We limited the bathroom to one person at a time via an Occupied/Free sign we found on Amazon (the CDC was FREAKED about bathroom infections). A favorite memory is the four of us and the dogs spending the day before the event (they flew in from the East Coast) sitting in our screened porch with our masks on, sometimes exchanging them for those plastic face shields. No one got sick. However, DD/DSIL and grands visited us this July and both DD and SIL caught Covid for the first time right after.", "images": []}

So of course I told him we'd cancel our tickets\u2014but we didn't need to; a day or two later, Broadway closed down. title: Recommend your arbor for climbing rose | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "pezhead439", "author_name": "pezhead439", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/pezhead439", "date": "2022-11-12", "text": "Hi. I'm in the market for a new arbor. Current one is a very weathered wooden one, and I'm about to plant Malvern Hills next year to grow up it. I'm concerned it'll overwhelm the existing structure, which already has a honeysuckle (the native one, that isn't quite as vigorous) growing up the other side... may or may not keep the honeysuckle. I'd love to get a powder-coated metal arbor but every one I find is either super expensive or the reviews say they rust. Anyone have a good arbor they've liked and could recommend? I need something fairly substantial. I've got enough room for something in the 4-6 ft width and depth range. My thinking is it's better to replace the arbor now before investing time and effort growing a new rose on it, and then have it rot out from under it. TIA for your advice!", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "fig-insanity", "author_name": "fig_insanity Z7b E TN", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/fig-insanity", "date": "2022-11-14", "text": "This is my favorite, built of rebar, no welding required. I built one for my mom, but tripled the depth of the one in the diagram below. This isn't mine, photo credit goes to FamilyHandyman. Check out his photos of the finished arbor. The instructions are here at FamilyHandyman Arbor. His photo shows two unconnected arches installed close to each other, but not touching.  It uses two sizes of rebar, and copper wire. You'll need a good hacksaw, and a conduit bender. I tripled the depth from a single arch of 12\", to a connected single unit totaling 3 feet by making two arbors per the instructions and connecting them with yet another set of rebar circles between them, making the arbor about 36\" deep. So if you choose to do that, you'll need enough of each size rebar to make another arbor per the instructions, plus another section of 3/8\" rebar for the extra circles. Theoretically, you could make the arbor as deep as you wanted by adding more sections. You'd just need to make sure to reinforce across all the sections with straight horizontal pieces of rebar the total length of the arbor (read below). I did the final assembly where I wanted to place the arbor, and it's a good thing I did: once it was assembled, it wanted to flex quite a bit...it's also HEAVY. So on both sides I added long straight pieces of rebar horizontally below the lowest circles, and again at the height of the bend where the arch begins (head high), as reinforcement. Once I did that, and sank the feet into the ground, it's strong enough I think it would support anything but the worst of house-eating ramblers. It's VERY sturdy. I'd use the thickest copper wire you can find (or can afford! lol) as it ages to a lovely blue green verdigris. Also, take care to be neat about wrapping/winding it (Family Handyman was kind of messy with his, lol), as it WILL show until the roses have grown over the arbor. But I consider that a feature, not a bug. That's why I suggest the thicker wire, as it will be more decorative. Mom's arbor is now three years old, has two maturing Edens on it, and was a sight to behold this Spring, even though the roses only reached about halfway up ( a stray cane or two reached higher). I'm hoping this coming year they reach the top. I'll take pix if they do, lol. EDIT: I forgot to mention that when I connected the two arches, I placed those middle-row rebar circles in alternating positions with the ones in the pre-made arches, so that they don't make straight horizontal rows across the sides of the arbor. In other words, the circles make a zig-zag across the sides of the arbor, one up-one down-one up. I used one more circle in the connecting row since I started one position lower, so the center row comes closer to the ground. I'm not sure I described that coherently, but feel free to ask for clarification if you're interested, lol. EDIT 2: I installed Mom's arbor in April, when the ground was soaking wet. I just pushed the feet into the soil, pushing each side of the arbor in by just a couple of inches, moving to the other side, repeating until they were all sufficiently deep. It would have been LOTS easier with more than one person. If you were to install one in dry or hard ground, I'd pre-punch the holes go by driving a spare piece of rebar into the ground where the feet will go. You'd have to be careful to make the holes vertical, and close to where the arbor is assembled, so you don't have to move the dang heavy thing very far. Be sure the hole-punching rebar is long enough for you to have enough to grab and pull it back out!", "images": ["https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/43e23fdc03729316_3144-w240-h399-b0-p0--.jpg"]}}

main_question: {"author_id": "prajeeth-wilton", "author_name": "Prajeeth Wilton", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/prajeeth-wilton", "date": "2022-11-13", "text": "Hello,I have the following quotes here in Edmonton, AB and looking for some advice on which I can go with.- Carrier 59TP6 [2-stage 80k btu 96% eff]- York TM9V060 [var speed 70k btu 96% eff]- Lennox EL296UH070XV36B [var speed 70k btu 96%]This is replacing a current 80k BTU Lennox Elite System.Thank you in advance", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "pfvwus-pf~312471206", "author_name": "Austin Air Companie", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/professionals/pfvwus-pf~312471206", "date": "2022-11-13", "text": "These furnaces are all essentially in the same class of furnaces 96% condensing, 2 stage, variable speed blower or ECM. (The mfgs reliably just copy one another more or less) Other differences can be control options (proprietary controls for specific brand, model etc) Algorithm chosen to control the machine. Product Warranty: More or less the same if the product is properly registered, properly installed etc. The primary difference is sizing as the Carrier you list is an 80K BTU as opposed to 60K BTU from the other choices (Lennox & York). I don't know specifically what size the Carrier is because the model number you provide is redacted that would include that info. You list it as an 80K BTU furnace. If you need the 80K BTU then the Carrier would be the better choice of the three. If your current furnace size is 60K BTU the duct work is probably sized for 60K BTU. It's not just about choosing a brand, it's also about choosing who you'll call when you need maintenance performed and or repairs. What is my favorite brand? One that is broken. Out of all these I really have no preference if sizing and ductwork and installation is properly done it really doesn't matter which brand. The reason to do this is that you will never find the pre-finished flooring you buy today when you want to make those future changes.  So you either need to buy it all now, or wait, or be prepared for what your plan to match future flooring will be. But I suspect you really just want a suggestion of what to actually buy.  That is so much a personal decision, and we have so little information about your situation. Personally, I would select something classic and timeless.  White or red oak.  Maybe natural maple.  Probably not hickory or anything exotic.  I would avoid anything gray, since that is supposed to be trending out.  And it isn't naturally occurring in most wood (OK, driftwood can be gray, but that is the exception that proves the rule!). A couple of things to know:  red oak can be red or orange or pink (orange and pink are just red with either yellow or white added!).  Maple will definitely yellow a bit (or a lot) over time. A medium brown color (not too dark, and not too light) is relatively classic and neutral, and will therefore work with whatever colors you use in decorating your home. I would select something in a medium width (3 or 4 inches) if you are doing solid hardwood.  Maybe 5 inches if you are in a climate without humidity. It has like 3 separate areas w with roots", "images": []}, "Comment 4": {"author_id": "lmecheverri", "author_name": "L Evve (Miami)", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/lmecheverri", "date": "2022-11-14", "text": "The last plant in which I noticed something similar after months didn\u2019t have one root\u2026 https://www.houzz.com/discussions/6312189/jade-plant-trunk", "images": []}, "Comment 5": {"author_id": "webuser-355114", "author_name": "tapla  (mid-Michigan, USDA z5b-6a)", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/webuser-355114", "date": "2022-11-14", "text": "If roots are growing, adopt a \"wait and see\" approach but avoid over-watering. Your plant is well protected by special substances in its skin (cuticular wax) that limit water loss through the periderm (outer skin). I would caution you about lifting the plant to examine roots or even tugging on it to check for resistance that indicates it has produced roots. The habit is very counterproductive because it breaks roots (some of them almost microscopic) and robs the plant of the food/ energy it takes to regenerate the roots killed. Using a 'tell' Over-watering saps vitality and is one of the most common plant assassins, so learning to avoid it is worth the small effort. Plants make and store their own energy source \u2013 photosynthate - (sugar/glucose). Functioning roots need energy to drive their metabolic processes, and in order to get it, they use oxygen to burn (oxidize) their food. From this, we can see that terrestrial plants need plenty of air (oxygen) in the soil to drive root function. Many off-the-shelf soils hold too much water and not enough air to support the kind of root health most growers would like to see; and, a healthy root system is a prerequisite to a healthy plant. Watering in small sips leads to avoid over-watering leads to a residual build-up of dissolved solids (salts) in the soil from tapwater and fertilizer solutions, which limits a plant's ability to absorb water \u2013 so watering in sips simply moves us to the other horn of a dilemma. It creates another problem that requires resolution. Better, would be to simply adopt a soil that drains well enough to allow watering to beyond the saturation point, so we're flushing the soil of accumulating dissolved solids whenever we water; this, w/o the plant being forced to pay a tax in the form of reduced vitality, due to prolong periods of soil saturation. Sometimes, though, that's not a course we can immediately steer, which makes controlling how often we water a very important factor. In many cases, we can judge whether or not a planting needs watering by hefting the pot. This is especially true if the pot is made from light material, like plastic, but doesn't work (as) well when the pot is made from heavier material, like clay, or when the size/weight of the pot precludes grabbing it with one hand to judge its weight and gauge the need for water. Fingers stuck an inch or two into the soil work ok for shallow pots, but not for deep pots. Deep pots might have 3 or more inches of soil that feels totally dry, while the lower several inches of the soil is 100% saturated. Obviously, the lack of oxygen in the root zone situation can wreak havoc with root health  and cause the loss of a very notable measure of your plant's potential. Inexpensive watering meters don't even measure moisture levels, they measure electrical conductivity. Clean the tip and insert it into a cup of distilled water and witness the fact it reads 'DRY'. One of the most reliable methods of checking a planting's need for water is using a 'tell'. You can use a bamboo skewer in a pinch, but a wooden dowel rod of about 5/16\u201d (75-85mm) would work better. They usually come 48\u201d (120cm) long and can usually be cut in half and serve as a pair. Sharpen all 4 ends in a pencil sharpener and slightly blunt the tip so it's about the diameter of the head on a straight pin. Push the wooden tell deep into the soil. Don't worry, it won't harm the root system. If the plant is quite root-bound, you might need to try several places until you find one where you can push it all the way to the pot's bottom. Leave it a few seconds, then withdraw it and inspect the tip for moisture. For most plantings, withhold water until the tell comes out dry or nearly so. If you see signs of wilting, adjust the interval between waterings so drought stress isn't a recurring issue. Al", "images": []}}

other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "buehl", "author_name": "Buehl", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/buehl", "date": "2022-11-14", "text": "Regarding a \"local custom cabinetmaker\"...do not assume they are out of your price range BUT also do not assume they are any better or even as good as other cabinetmakers. From one of the links in the \"New to Kitchens?  Read Me First!\" thread: Local Custom Cabinetmakers -- Good or Bad? This topic comes up now and then, so I am posting what I've posted in the past. In addition, see this thread (https://www.gardenweb.com/discussions/2679023/custom-cabinets-really-cheaper-than-stock) and the post from GreenDesigns about half-way down. ++++++++++++++++++++ Just a word of caution...\"local (custom) cabinetmaker\" is thrown around here a lot with the implication they are superior to the various cabinet manufacturers. They may be, but there is no guarantee. \"Local custom cabinetmaker\" does not necessarily equate to \"high quality\" or \"low cost\". There are many very good custom cabinetmakers out there, but there are many not-so-good ones as well. Just b/c someone is a \"custom cabinetmaker\" does not make him/her a good cabinetmaker. And, it's not just their skill at cabinetry...how are their business skills? E.g., How are they at meeting schedules? Do they stay within the cost they quote you? How do they deal with issues? What is their warranty? What recourse do you have if they drop the ball? Sometimes you can go \"over the heads\" of people at cabinet stores or even go to the manufacturer (at least for warranty issues), but you might not have that option with a local cabinetmaker. If you go this route, be very diligent in your research: These are all the same questions you should ask of a manufacturing line as well, but all these things are usually spelled out somewhere and they have staff who specialize in these areas. You usually have some \"standard\" recourses if there are problems. In addition, their quality, including finishes and construction, are generally pretty consistent (yes, there are glitches occasionally) and they have the advantage for those finishes that are better when manufactured than when done by hand. I'm not saying don't look into local cabinetmakers, I'm saying be careful. We have had several threads where people have gone this route and have had major issues in all the areas above...construction quality, finish quality, installation issues, difficult to work with, etc. And yes, there have been similar threads from those using cabinet companies (but those are usually resolved fairly quickly once the person gets up the courage to say something.) title: Autumn/Thanksgiving: Decor, Food, Events, Plans, Problems, Stories. | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "internet1382", "author_name": "Aphaea", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/internet1382", "date": "2022-11-14", "text": "I have been waiting (and waiting) for a discussion to pop up on this this time of the year. I love it, going a bit overboard with holiday feelings. These last three+ months of the year are sheer joy for me. Do you love it like I do? Are you more than ready for it after the last two seasons were badly affected by Covid? Are you still taking precautions? Have you decorated? Show us with plenty of pictures! Are you planning your Thanksgiving menu, or if you are in Canada, what did you do for Thanksgiving? Will you share it with us? What is traditional with you? Do you buy pumpkins or put out faux ones? Do you decorate the outside? The inside? Do you add seasonal fall decor to your usual look or do you exchange items so as not to overwhelm your space? Do you have pets who like to mess with these \"new\" objects? What do you use and where do you use it? Does your whole house get decorated or do you put out only minimal decorations in a single room? What kinds of things do you like? What do you stay away from? What is your family or friends gathering like, or what was it like? Are there issues or problems you will or did grapple with? Were there any kitchen disasters? Are rising prices making you re-think what you will serve? Will it be a small gathering or are you part of a large one? If it's at your house, do you clean madly or just shrug and say \"if it's clean enough for me, it's clean enough for my guests?\" Do any guests stay overnight? Any funny or frustrating stories there? Any questions or issues we can help you with? Is it an exhausting holiday for you? Do you participate in the mad shopping sales that weekend? Or do you wait a day or more to change over from autumn decor to holiday (winter or Christmas) decor? How do you put autumn/Thanksgiving decor away? Do you pack it all away in labeled boxes or kind of toss it into bags or old boxes and in the garage or the attic? Please . . . tell us all! We are ready, we're asking, and we really want to know. Shower us with pictures, stories, annoyances, menus, recipes. Now, for me, I live alone (with three cats) but I am so crazy about this time of the year. It takes an enormous amount of effort to make myself wait until October 1 to bring out the autumn decorations. I do not like Halloween so I don't have anything for that. I love pumpkins so I have about 15 faux ones (glass, ceramic, mercury glass, copper, resin, fabric, velvet, paper and more) from large ones that work on the floor to fingernail-sized wool ones. I often add real ones in white, pink, and green, especially if they are \"flawed\" with bumps and such. The top of my living room open bookcase/display case mostly empty on top, gets covered in a faux autumn leaf garlands and pumpkins. So does the top of the smaller bookcases in the alcove reading/meditation area of the den. I also have a couple of vintage Thanksgiving postcards that are framed and set among the pumpkins. A couple of pumpkins are in the bedroom on the dresser. And inside my oversized vintage hand-painted Italian coffee table, in the bottom level, the drawer, is the dried wheat that I could barely keep away from the cats while deciding where to put it. As I have gotten older my menu has gotten easier. No more of the massive meal especially as the guest list has shrunk. This year, I bought the turkey breast from Trader Joe's that is cooked and just needs heating. I made my tart cranberry sauce, will make gravy and stuffing and will buy some nice green beans, buy a couple of TJ's pre-made salads to throw into a bowl and add a homemade dressing plus, of course, a pumpkin pie. I do not shop but I take down the autumn/Thanksgiving decorations and lovingly put them away and store them neatly in the shed. In addition, since Friday still \"belongs\" to Thanksgiving for me I spend time quietly that day: a walk, meditation, playing with the cats, maybe browse a few home websites. It's the end of the first part of my favorite three month seasonal joy so I savor what I had and a bit of what's to come. Tell me ALL about yours!", "images": []}

title: Robin Red Holly not producing berries | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "ajay-singh116", "author_name": "AJ Princeton NJ z6b", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/ajay-singh116", "date": "2022-11-14", "text": "I live in New Jersey, Zone 6b. Last fall (Oct 2021) I planted a row of eight Holly trees about 5-6 feet in height. These were the Robin Red variety. They are supposed to be more deer resistant than Nellie Stevens and also have a darker green color. This spring I saw some winter burn - but all Hollie trees did well and even showed about a foot of growth. But the surprise is that there are no red berries. Now the Red Robin cultivar is supposed to be a female only cultivar which doesn\u2019t require a male Holly close by in order to produce berries. So I have read. I have an older large 20 foot tall Nellie Stevens near by which is laden with red berries. But none of the new Hollies have any berries. What do you suppose is going on.. other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "nandina-gw", "author_name": "nandina", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/nandina-gw", "date": "2022-11-23", "text": "Glad to give you a helping hand, AJ. My Dad was a well-known Ilex authority and holly hybridizers would send him various samples of their hybridizing efforts to be planted and trialed at our nursery before introduction to the trade. It is a simple process. Wait until a holly comes into spring bloom, then push a blossom's petals apart so you can carefully look into the center of the blossom. If it is a female, you should be able to see a tiny green berry forming in the middle section of each blossom, which will develop into a mature berry in the fall. Here is a great example of a proper reveal on a frameless cabinet with a similar set up to the OP  This is a stacked crown and the OP doesn't need that, but the reveals are done properly.   Notice how if the doors are open the crown would appear much larger on the front.  That is because the reveal is pulled out in the front to align with the doors rather than the box.  This is what should be done when the side panels are pulled flush with the doors giving an inset appearance.  Alternatively, if the side panels are not pulled flush with the doors, you can add some height and use a standard reveal but you want the crown a bit above the doors then to add separation. To answer your questions as best I can.  Generally speaking, a cost plus contract is all costs reasonable and necessary, so a contractor can't profit from his mistakes.  But neither can you.  Suppose you ask for an upgraded tile and the contractor never gets you the price of that upgrade but does the work and you agree it is nice. The contractor then presents you with a bill that is much higher than expected.  You still have to pay for the upgraded tile as it is unreasonable to expect that you should have the upgraded tile for free, however, you might get the contractor's percentage removed as that is profiting from his mistake, especially if you argue that you would have made a different decision were you given the actual price. This is the problem with overages that violate the specific terms of the contract.  You still had the work done and should have reasonably expected to pay for additional work.  However, items that should have been included in the original bid but were omitted are generally considered his mistake and shouldn't trigger an additional charge, but there is a lot of nuance to this because of unjust enrichment and damages.  So it might be best to say... it depends. title: Can chicken grit be used instead of perlite for vegetable containers? | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "webuser-133314901", "author_name": "HU-133314901", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/webuser-133314901", "date": "2022-11-15", "text": "With my succulents, it's really worked to replace perlite with chicken grit (and pea gravel). Cheaper, better visual aesthetics (IMO) and it does not float to the top when watered. It is heavier, but manageable in the pot sizes I use. Is it a valid option when growing oragnic vegetables in containers?", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "daninthedirt", "author_name": "daninthedirt (USDA 9a, HZ9, CentTX, Sunset z30, Cfa)", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/daninthedirt", "date": "2022-11-15", "text": "Perlite soaks up water and air, helping to moisten and aerate soil. it also helps with drainage. Chicken grit and pea gravel don't do the former, but do help with the latter. I should add that succulents hoard water in their leaves, and as a result are very drought tolerant and even like the soil to dry out occasionally. They don't need the soil to be kept moist. In this respect, perlite is sort of overkill with them. But succulents do need the soil to drain well, and chicken grit and pea gravel should do that just as well. Most vegetables, however, like their soil to be moist.", "images": []}, "Comment 2": {"author_id": "jodigoatmom", "author_name": "JodiK", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/jodigoatmom", "date": "2022-11-16", "text": "I'm a big proponent of using a medium that is larger in particulate than the silt sold as potting soil, the aeration and draining of the former which promotes better, healthier root growth, a must for any plant in a container... regardless of its type or variety. So, while I do sometimes utilize coarse perlite as one of the medium ingredients, the others consist of pine bark fines, chicken grit in the form of granite chips, akadama, turface, pea gravel, or any other inert ingredient of similar size. The particulate size of all ingredients being similar in size is of more importance than what they are, there being many substitutes out there, use depending on what is available. In essence, I use a version of what is known as \"Gritty Mix\" for all of my container grown plants, most of which are indoor houseplants. These range from cacti to bulbs, and even orchids. In my opinion, perlite doesn't absorb enough moisture to use it for that reason. I find that the pine bark fines do that portion of the heavy lifting much more efficiently. And truth be told, we don't want too much moisture to languish anywhere within that container for too long a period of time, or else the roots may literally drown without some oxygen. and the exchange of gases and oxygen via watering... gases from the decomposition of the pine bark fines and any other such matter that's a part of the mixture. I do adjust ingredient ratios depending on plant type, pot size, and other factors... but I take my cues from such areas of growing as bonsai, for example. Bonsai uses a larger particulate in conjunction with root pruning and careful watering to obtain good results. Aesthetics are less important than root health, without which there cannot be decent plant health above the soil surface. And all things being equal, I rather find the look of a good \"Gritty Mix\" to be rather pleasing. For visual appeal, I sometimes arrange a few small marbles or found fossil stones around the plant. Hope this helps! Happy Gardening!", "images": []}}

other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "kaseki", "author_name": "kaseki", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/kaseki", "date": "2022-11-15", "text": "Wolf hoods are available with internal, in-line, and exterior blowers. Download and review the Wolf Design Guide for examples.  Other manufacturers likely have similar data on the web sites. Please understand that the reason higher hoods require more flow rate (CFM) is that they need to have larger entry apertures to capture the rising and expanding cooking plumes.  Hoods do not pull up cooking plumes from the cooking surfaces, except for the most un-energetic cooking.  They entrain cooking plumes that enter the hoods into the hoods' baffle slots.  Unsuccessful capture and containment can occur due to the plumes reflecting out of the hoods and into the room volume. Hoods have very modest volumes below their base that have significant effect on deviating plume direction, depending somewhat on flow restrictions about the hood.  Compare island hood, wall hood without adjacent cabinets, and wall hood with adjacent cabinets, or side curtains, for how flow might be affected by constraining the flow paths. For lowest noise, use a remote blower and put a silencer in the path between hood and blower. Choose a hood that overlaps the cooking surfaces by the tangent of 10 degrees times the hood height, with some additional overlap beyond 36 inches to accommodate unavoidable drafts and people-motion turbulence.  With that area defined, multiply the intake area in sq. ft. by 90 CFM/sq. ft. to determine CFM required by most residential hoods to ensure containment.  Multiply by an additional factor of 1.5 to specify rated CFM of the blower.  This accounts for mainly baffle and duct pressure loss.  Depending on make-up air (MUA) system design, more \"excess\" blower rating may be needed. Normal maximum for residential hoods is 6 ft from the floor.  Commercial hoods are sized for 7 feet above the floor.  They are typically significantly larger than residential hoods.  Their working environment is more turbulent, and their cooking surfaces can be larger. Whatever was blooming. Somehow, things have changed. Two and three years ago we had wet summers (and the rest of the years weren't dry months, either). The trees, big old trees have grown.  Some down along the road have added twenty feet of hight and hide our view of the Smokey Mountains until leaf drop. This year is just ornery. August had two inches of rain, all of it the first week, September had 1.7 October said \"hold my beer\" and had 1.46 inches.  That rainfall didn't shut down the Noisettes, but the rest of the roses slowed remarkably and (we have a well) we began to worry about stressing the well.  The roses for the most part didn't make many buds at all. Now we've already had light freezes. We are forecast to have six nights in the low 20's.  Maybe Old Blush will come through, she has before.  But I wonder what this will do for the plants' overall health. There were fall days when the cold stayed up north and the shortened days going into December meant very few buds were being formed.  This year is going to be a very different kick to the roses' instinctive slow down going into winter.  We are wet.  I guess it's good that it's a cold wet as fungal problems don't seem to appear when the temps are consistently below 50. Several years ago I asked Lynette (In B.C.) if there would be roses blooming near her if we went to western Canada for Thanksgiving. title: Fertilize roses, yes or no? | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "seniorballoon", "author_name": "SeniorBalloon", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/seniorballoon", "date": "2022-11-16", "text": "Somewhat new to rose growing. Some of them I've never fertilized, a Westerland and a Nightowl, both grow like crazy. We bought a bunch of Roses last year from https://www.northlandrosarium.com/ and they doing great. This year was their second year and we did fertilize those, they grew well also. We are 97.3 % organic gardeners and we use an organic rose fertilizer. Been reading about the Soil Food Web and wondering if people are going no fertilizer with roses these days? Thanks, sb", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "starwarsfan89436", "author_name": "starwarsfan89436", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/starwarsfan89436", "date": "2022-11-16", "text": "After the first year of growth, you\u2019ll want to start your fertilizing process as soon as you\u2019re able to start working the soil. You\u2019ll keep fertilizing throughout the season unless you\u2019re using a slow-release granular fertilizer. As you near the end of the season, most northern gardeners stop fertilizing about eight weeks before you might experience a frost. This doesn\u2019t have to be exact, but it is a good way to allow the rose to prepare for winter and reduce any potential frost damage that would stress the plant out before going dormant. If you live in a zone that typically doesn\u2019t see frost, your rose will still probably go dormant for a couple of months, so stop fertilizing about eight weeks before typical dormancy times. This is likely closer to October or even November. The most important thing to do is purchase a high-quality rose fertilizer and then read the instructions on the packaging. This will give your rose the best chances at getting the nutrients it needs without giving it too much of a good thing. It also makes it easier if you\u2019re not an experienced rose gardener to keep your roses blooming and beautiful. I would suggest: Miracle Gro (https://amzn.to/3GlidDU) or Bio Advanced(https://amzn.to/3GmTkHW)", "images": []}}

title: Massive volunteer tomato bush - save seeds? | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "jacqueline9ca", "author_name": "jacqueline9CA", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/jacqueline9ca", "date": "2022-11-16", "text": "I had a volunteer tomato emerge this Spring in a bed where it has been at least 20+ years since I had a tomato bush. Those were Early Girls, but this one was NOT. Someone told me that Early Girl is a complex hybrid which of course does not come true to its own seed.  I get that. The tomato which emerged in my rose bed (climbing up a rose, of course) grew massively - within a month it had eaten 2 rose bushes, and within 2 months it had expanded to cover 4 of them, and by this time the tomato bush was easily 5 feet deep, 5 feet tall, and 10 feet wide. It bloomed and set fruit endlessly, and would have expanded to block the driveway except that the vehicles kept \"pruning\" it. I have been picking clusters of ripe tomatoes (each about the size of a ping pong ball) off it for months - perhaps 10 tomatoes per day would suddenly be truly ripe, and they were delicious. Happiness. So, I am presuming this was an old sort of tomato - the fruit was definitely too fragile to ship, and I learned to cut the clusters off, instead of trying for individual tomatoes, so as to keep them intact. My question is: I have never had much luck rooting anything from seed, except of course self seeding flowers or weeds, which also self seed. Sorry I am so ignorant, but does anyone know how to dry tomato seeds, and then what to do with them to get another plant or two? Do you need lots of complicated machinery? How do you prevent them from \"damping off\"? Of course there may be seeds underneath where the plant was (it is freezing here every night and the tomatoes are not ripening anymore, so I had my gardeners take out the bush today. It was laden with green tomatoes, of course, and they asked if they could take them home - they come from a So American culture which has LOTS of recipes for green tomatoes, and were very happy when I said yes. However, because we have a resident doe which discovered she liked the taste of tomato leaves about a week ago, I would like to grow a bush next year in my fully gated new rose garden. Can I just wait until a sprout comes up naturally and then dig it up and move it? Sorry this is so long with so many questions, but I grow a lot of roses, and hardly any vegetables. Any ideas would be really appreciated. Jackie", "images": []}

title: Question on coco chips | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "mr-bill_m", "author_name": "Bill M.", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/mr-bill_m", "date": "2022-11-17", "text": "I am thinking of changing my substrate over to coco chips. Don't ask why, but I'll tell you anyway - I'm bored. I'm thinking it might be some good therapy to repot some of my hoyas, and a few orchids as well, over to coco chips. Amazon has coco chips, charcoal and large pearlite (a threefer package) for $54. I think I may get it then slowly over the winter do some repotting. Right now my plants reside in orchid bark with some cactus soil and the fine pearlite sold in the big box stores. The selection on amazon looks to be a lot better. The question is - have any of you gone with coco chips? If so, which do you recommend, if any. What has your results been? Thoughts? Suggestions? Thanks....", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "webuser-355114", "author_name": "tapla  (mid-Michigan, USDA z5b-6a)", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/webuser-355114", "date": "2022-11-17", "text": "Coco chips (CHCs) and coir are physically and chemically different enough from peat and pine bark that they shouldn't be considered to be interchangeable without addressing their differences. This is something I wrote more than 10 years ago after trying coir and CHCs as significant fractions of container media: Sphagnum peat and coir have nearly identical water retention curves. They both retain about 90-95% of their volume in water at saturation and release it over approximately the same curve until they both lock water up so tightly it's unavailable for plant uptake at about 30-33% saturation. Coir actually has less loft than sphagnum peat, and therefore, less aeration. Because of this propensity, coir should be used in mixes at lower %s than peat. Because of its tendency to compact severely, coir is primarily used by the greenhouse industry in containers in sub-irrigation (bottom-watering) situations. Many sources produce coir that is high in soluble salts, so this can also be an issue. Using coir as the primary component of container media virtually eliminates lime or dolomitic lime as a possible Ca source because of coir's high pH (6+). Gypsum should be used as a Ca source, which effectively eliminates coir's low S content. All coir products are very high in K, very low in Ca, and have a potentially high Mn content, which can interfere with the uptake of Fe. Several studies have also shown that the significant presence of phenolic allelochemicals in fresh coir can be very problematic for a high % of plants, causing poor growth and reduced yields. I haven't tested coir thoroughly, but I have done some testing of CHCs (coconut husk chips) with some loose controls in place. After very thoroughly leaching and rinsing the chips, I made a 5:1:1 soil of pine bark:peat:perlite (which I know to be very productive) and a 5:1:1 mix of CHCs:peat:perlite. I planted 6 cuttings of snapdragon and 6 cuttings of Coleus (each from the same plant to help reduce genetic influences) in containers (same size/shape) of the different soils. I added dolomitic lime to the bark soil and gypsum to the CHC soil. After the cuttings struck, I eliminated all but the three strongest in each of the 4 containers. I watered each container with a weak solution of MG 12-4-8 with STEM added at each watering, and watered on an 'as needed basis', not on a schedule. The only difference in the fertilizer regimen was the fact that I included a small amount of MgSO4 (Epsom salts) to provide Mg (the dolomitic lime in the bark soil contained the MG, while the gypsum [CaSO4] in the CHC soil did not. This difference was necessary because or the high pH of CHCs and coir.) for the CHC soil. The results were startling. In both cases, the cuttings grown in the CHC's were chlorotic and exhibited < 1/2 the biomass at summers end as the plants in the bark mix. The same occurred when substituting coir for peat in the 5:1:1 mix. I just find it very difficult for a solid case to be made (besides \"It works for me\") for the use of coir or CHC's. They're more expensive and more difficult to use effectively. The fact that some believe peat is in short supply (no where near true, btw) is easily offset by the effect of the carbon footprint of coir in its trek to the US from Sri Lanka or other exotic locales. That's the view from here. YMMV Coir Study: https://sites.google.com/site/plantandsoildigest/usu-crop-physiology-laboratory/coconut-coir-studies Al", "images": []}}

title: Granite supplier sold our fantasy brown slab...what to do?! | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "webuser-643008993", "author_name": "Zippy Dudar", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/webuser-643008993", "date": "2022-11-17", "text": "Photo: shows 6 slabs of the lot we were assured our counters would be cut from 2 of these slabs  hi - if you're going to answer in a snide or snarky way, please just don't. My Mom is turning 93 on Tuesday. For the first time in 30+ years her kitchen is being redone. She and I have planned it over a whole year. We took our time in finding precisely what we wanted and getting good workers (hard to find in rural New Hampshire). Cabinets were backordered 5.5 months, but arrived in perfect shape--even more gorgeous than we remembered and dreamed--they have been installed beautifully, and the fabricator was here Monday doing templating for the countertops. Counters scheduled to be installed 11/21, with plumbing hooked back up 11/22 (Mom's bday)--right in time for Thanksgiving. This spring I had traveled through 2 states to lab yards and stone suppliers to find exactly the Fantasy Brown slabs right for us.  We even waited until we had found the perfect exact stone before finalizing cabinet vendor, colors, styles, lighting fixtures, etc. for the kitchen. We paid 50% back in June for the slabs--there were 6 available at the time. At the time we told the vendor we had selected them and these slabs because the Fantasy Brown was very light, that we do NOT like nor want dark browns in our kitchen, and has greenish blue waves that we adored  (which we matched not only exactly with our new island, but also we have painted that color below the chair rail in an adjoining dining room). In June when we said that--prior to buying--the woman told us this would be no problem because they would be cutting from 2 slabs, which she said were identical, like cutting a loaf of bread, and that we were not charged by the slab but the square foot, and would likely be using 2 slabs to get the light colors for our needs. This summer and early fall I called 2x - just to make sure the slabs were still there--and was assured they were. I even went by after hours (given how completely wonky everything has been during and post COVID) and saw for myself that 2 slabs marked \"SOLD\" were there in the yard, and even took pictures for my Mom and me to admire and excitedly await the cabs coming in and getting these beautiful Fantasy Brown counters! Wednesday (yesterday), as planned, we went to lay out the templates on the actual slabs. The blase, bored, patronizing young woman in minidress and thigh high boots drawled that the sink and adjoining part would have to be cut from X location. My Mom and I both said, actually, let's scoot it down a foot (and I showed her) to get the light colors and patterns. She rolled her eyes and said, Well, then you couldn't get all the rest of the stone you need for the other cabinets and island. I said \"I guess we'll have to do some of that from the other slab, as you'd mentioned this summer.\" \"Oh...if I said that...I don't remember. We're sold out of this lot. There's nothing left except this one slab.\" Are there other Fantasy Brown slabs available then? we ask. My Mom--in good shape, but 93 and it's sleeting outside in the dwindling light--and I follow the young woman who stomps out into the yard striding 30 feet in front of us, talking to the air and pointing at dark slabs after dark slabs. Nothing remotely like our gorgeous slab. She says \"Well, there's nothing I can do....this is what we have for you,\" flat-voiced and shrugging, looking at the clock. I said we would need to talk to someone else to help us figure out how to solve this. She said no one else was there but the sales manager would be in Thursday/today. I remember the sales manager and she was a clone of the supercilious unpleasant girl who petulantly \"helped\" us Wednesday. We are pretty sure he will say the same thing. \"Oh, no one should have told you we'd cut your counters from 2 slabs. We already sold the others.\" (Shrug) What should we do? What do we say? Whom do we talk to or ask for? What leverage do we have? What recourse? or what can we ask them to do for us? I already looked at the online inventory of the 2 suppliers they use (2 hours away, in Massachusetts). If their websites are current and updated (which they may not be) all the Fantasy Brown at both suppliers is dark. We do NOT want dark Fantasy Brown--the slab we love had only the bottom 20% dark We don't want that. It will not even GO with our kitchen and all we have selected, bought and had installed otherwise re: cabinetry and shelving etc.  It MAY be conceivable to get the L-shaped piece with the sink and range in it of the part of the slab we want and 2 of the others cabinet counters, but there is NO way the island can be cut from that same slab. I will ask if they have a remnant -- but clearly the remnant will not be cut from the same lot -- but maybe at least it will be lighter than all the dark stone currently on display in the slab yard. Any other thoughts? suggestions? Ideas? Thanks - sorry for long post - and thanks again (not to put too fine a point on this, but my very stoic Yankee Mom almost burst into tears on the drive home...it has been a long process of emptying everything out of her kitchen -- and us staying in a rental house until the construction is done -- and her birthday coming up and Thanksgiving, and this imploding....really, really disappointing)", "images": ["https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/0d528b7303760b4d_0531-w500-h319-b0-p0--.jpg", "https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/e2f2c02c0376eb28_7836-w500-h313-b0-p0--.jpg", "https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/d242c81e0376eb28_7833-w500-h666-b0-p0--.jpg", "https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/9f82e85b0376eb29_7839-w500-h390-b0-p0--.jpg", "https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/c372e3a00376eb2a_7840-w500-h375-b0-p0--.jpg"]}
